prompt: A fixed-multitape machine solves a problem in polynomial time. A general one-tape simulation stores all tapes together and sweeps that representation to simulate each step. What does its polynomial overhead establish?

options.text: Every one-tape algorithm has exactly the same runtime
options.explanation: Simulation preserves behaviour, but repeated sweeps can add work.

options.text: The overhead is unavoidable for this particular problem
options.explanation: An upper bound for one construction does not rule out a faster specialised algorithm.

options.text: The problem still has a polynomial-time one-tape algorithm, although the exponent may increase
options.explanation: Correct. Composing a polynomial runtime with polynomial simulation overhead remains polynomial.

options.text: Multiple tapes recognise languages that one tape cannot
options.explanation: The simulation establishes equal computational power; convenience can change speed.

workedExample:
1. Encode each tape and head position on one tape.
2. A sweep finds the scanned symbols and another pass can apply the changes.
3. The used representation grows with simulated work, producing polynomial overhead under the stated cost assumptions.
4. The resulting algorithm is still polynomial. This explains agreement of the polynomial-time class across these models, without claiming identical speed or a tight lower bound.

prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. A decider is in particular a recogniser that happens to always halt.

options.text: Nondeterministic TMs recognise more languages than deterministic TMs
options.explanation: They recognise exactly the same languages. A deterministic TM can simulate all branches breadth-first.

options.text: A TM with a two-way infinite tape recognises the same languages as one with a one-way tape
options.explanation: Correct. Fold the two-way tape in half and interleave the two sides on the one-way tape.

options.text: A recogniser for L must reject every string that is not in L
options.explanation: A recogniser may loop on strings outside L. Rejecting all of them is what makes it a decider.

options.text: If a TM halts on every input, the language it accepts is decidable
options.explanation: Correct. That is the definition of deciding a language.

workedExample:
1. Every decider is also a recogniser. True.
2. NTM and DTM: same class of languages, possibly exponentially different running times. False.
3. Two-way tape: simulate with tracks or interleaving. True.
4. Recognisers only need to accept the members of L. On non-members they may reject or loop. False.
5. Halting on all inputs is precisely the decider condition. True.

prompt: You simulate a nondeterministic TM with a deterministic one. Why does ordinary breadth-first search work where unbounded depth-first traversal may fail?

options.explanation: Memory is not the issue; the problem is correctness.

options.text: Depth-first might follow an infinite non-accepting branch forever and never reach an accepting branch elsewhere, so it could fail to accept strings the NTM accepts
options.explanation: Correct. Breadth-first visits every node at depth d before depth d + 1, so an accepting leaf at finite depth is always found.

options.text: Breadth-first is faster, making the simulation polynomial
options.explanation: The breadth-first simulation is still exponential in the worst case. Its advantage is completeness, not speed.

options.text: There is no reason; either order works
options.explanation: Depth-first can go wrong whenever some branch runs forever, which TMs are allowed to do.

workedExample:
1. Nondeterministic acceptance requires some accepting branch, possibly beside an infinite branch.
2. Unbounded depth-first traversal may stay on the infinite branch forever.
3. Breadth-first traversal visits every node at each finite depth before moving deeper. Finite branching makes each level finite.
4. Any accepting node has a finite depth, so it is eventually reached. Iterative deepening is another fair approach.
5. This establishes correct recognition, not an efficient algorithm: the number of explored branches can grow exponentially.

prompt: A Turing machine halts after exactly t steps on an input of length n. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The head visited at most one more cell than the number of steps
options.explanation: Correct. It starts on one cell and each step moves to at most one new cell.

options.text: The final non-blank cell count is at most the input length plus the step count
options.explanation: Correct. Initially n cells are non-blank; each step writes at most one cell, so at most t more become non-blank.

options.text: The runtime is at least the input length, because every input symbol must be read
options.explanation: A TM can reject immediately after inspecting a wrong first symbol. It need not read every input cell, so runtime can be less than input length.

options.text: The machine could have used infinitely many tape cells
options.explanation: Each step reaches at most one new cell, so a finite step count bounds the visited cells. Infinite tape is available, but every finite run uses finitely much.

options.text: Some configuration must have repeated during the run
options.explanation: A repeated configuration of a deterministic TM means an infinite loop. A halting run never repeats a configuration.

workedExample:
1. The head starts on one cell and can reach at most one new cell per step, giving the visited-cell bound.
2. Each step writes at most one cell, so the final nonblank cells cannot exceed the initial input cells plus the number of steps.
3. A machine may halt after seeing an invalid first symbol; reading the entire input is not mandatory.
4. A finite run cannot visit infinitely many cells.
5. A repeated complete configuration in a deterministic machine would repeat the entire future and prevent halting. Repeated states alone do not imply this.
